Editorial: choosing an appropriate risk stratification tool for 
nonalcoholic fatty liver disease—one size does not fit all
Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a global epidemic affect-
ing ~25% of the world population.1 Liver fibrosis stage is the main 
predictor of NAFLD complications, including decompensated cirrho-
sis, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), liver transplant and mortality.2 
Therefore, recent efforts have increasingly focused on risk strati-
fying NAFLD patients to identify NAFLD patients with significant 
fibrosis.3
Kang and colleagues assessed the utility of evaluating a 
large cohort of individuals attending health check-up clinics in 
South Korea with magnetic resonance elastography (MRE).4 
After excluding patients with chronic liver disease (CLD) causes 
other than NAFLD, they found that 8.0% of their NAFLD cohort 
(n = 413) had significant liver fibrosis, while 1.5% had advanced 
fibrosis. However, among the average risk population without ev-
idence of CLD or NAFLD, significant and advanced fibrosis were 
2.1% and 0.2%, respectively. These findings highlight the burden 
of liver fibrosis secondary to NAFLD in this study patient cohort.
Different modalities can be used to evaluate liver fibrosis.5 
Although MRE is considered the most accurate modality, it is costly 
and not widely available. Transient elastography (TE), although 
accurate and commonly used, is mainly limited to tertiary referral 
centres. Therefore, recent studies have recommended implement-
ing serum-based fibrosis scores, such as fibrosis-4 variable index 
(FIB-4), as a first step in evaluating NAFLD patients for advanced 
fibrosis in primary care. However, using FIB-4 alone leads to ~ 30% 
of NAFLD patients requiring liver specialist assessment.3 Optimally, 
serum fibrosis score testing can be followed by an elastography 
based modality, such as TE, shearwave elastography (SWE) or MRE.3
The current study is similar to previously published popula-
tion-based studies using radiological methods as a first step to 
identify NAFLD patients with either significant or advanced fibro-
sis.6-9 Caballeria et al reported that 5.8% of the general Barcelona 
population had LSM by TE >8.0 kPa, with the majority of patients 
having NAFLD. In contrast, Koehler et al reported a prevalence of 
8.4% for the same LSM cut-off in a Dutch population.6,8 A study 
from Hong Kong reported that 2% of NAFLD patients in the general 
population had LSM >9.6 kPa.7 However, all of these studies used 
LSM measured by TE for estimating liver fibrosis, differing from 
the current study. The current study does have some important 
limitations, including 81% of cohort participants were men and me-
dian BMI was 25 kg/m2. 
Recent guidelines have recommended an enhanced focus on risk 
stratification of NAFLD patients at a population level, to assess the 
utility and cost-effectiveness of case-identification of patients with 
either significant or advanced fibrosis.10 With promising antifibrotic 
therapies coming to the clinic soon, coupled with current recommen-
dations for intense lifestyle modification, there is an urgent need to 
develop clinical pathways that robustly risk-stratify NAFLD patients 
based on fibrosis stage. Each pathway should implement serum-based 
and/or radiological modalities based on locally available resources.

Editorial: choosing an appropriate risk stratification tool for 
nonalcoholic fatty liver disease—one size does not fit all. 
Authors' reply
We appreciate the opportunity to reply to the valid points that 
Shaheen and Swain raised about our recent study on the use 
of magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) to determine the 
presence of fibrosis in the general population and those with 
NAFLD.1,2 In particular, they pointed out that MRE is an expen-
sive technology that is not as readily available in clinical prac-
tice settings as ultrasound or serum biomarkers which weakens 
our study results. In fact, they suggest, as does another recent 
review of non-invasive methods to determine the presence of 
fibrosis, that serum biomarkers should be used as the first line 
of diagnosis and then patients may need to be referred out for 
ultrasound or MRE if the serum results indicate the possible pres-
ence of fibrosis.2,3
We do not disagree with the authors and feel that our study 
only strengthens the use of ultrasound as a first line, nonserum 
based diagnostic tool since our results were similar to other re-
ported results that used ultrasound as their diagnostic method as 
the authors pointed out.4-6 However, it is important to remember 
that the discordance between the results obtained using MRE and 
ultrasound increases when the patient's BMI increases such that 
MRE is the more accurate diagnostic method.3 In our study, approx-
imately 25% of the population was considered obese (BMI ≥27.5) 
while the majority were considered overweight with an average 
BMI of 25.7 ± 3.2 kg/m2, suggesting that MRE would be the most 
appropriate diagnostic method which further strengthens our study 
results.3,7
Furthermore, though the majority of our population was male, 
this finding is also in line with the majority of reports on persons with 
NAFLD.8 In addition, gender was not found to be a significant pre-
dictor in our multivariate analysis for the variables associated with 
fibrosis while age (P = 0.001), decreased platelet count (P = 0.001), 
increased AST/ALT ratio (P = 0.022), presence of diabetes (P = 0.006), 
and presence of fatty liver on MR (P = 0.001) were all independent 
risk factors for significant fibrosis.
We agree that developing an appropriate guideline to iden-
tify those at risk for NAFLD and then to appropriately risk stratify 
those identified with NAFLD for further fibrosis assessment is much 
needed especially as the rate of NAFLD continues to grow along 
with its economic burden.10 The role of MRE in population screening 
will need continued study; however, as our study has shown, MRE 
provides an accurate measurement of NAFLD-related fibrosis and 
should be considered a viable option especially in a population that 
is overweight or obese.
